extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets and literary critics (readers interested in principles of poetry and poetic criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive statements about what poetry is, what its aims should be, and who is competent to judge it; guidance on poetic style (music, delicacy, imagination) and anti-patterns (over-metaphysical, overly learned poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique quality correlates with poetical talent
rubrics_metrics.description: “It has been said that a good critique on a poem may be written by one who is no poet himself. This... I feel to be false—the less poetical the critic, the less just the critique, and the converse.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic's justice in judging poetry increases with his poetical talent; non-poets and bad poets are liable to make false critiques. The passage argues that intimate acquaintance with poetic craft gives a critic special insight that offsets partialities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets can (often) judge their own work
rubrics_metrics.description: “I think the notion that no poet can form a correct estimate of his own writings is another [vulgar error]. ...a poet, who is indeed a poet, could not, I think, fail of making a just critique; whatever should be deducted on the score of self-love might be replaced on account of his intimate acquaintance with the subject.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-critique by a genuinely talented poet is defensible because intimate knowledge of one’s art may compensate for vanity. Caveat: the author admits exceptions (e.g., Milton) and recognizes more instances of false self-critique among lesser poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate object of poetry is pleasure, not truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “A poem, in my opinion, is opposed to a work of science by having, for its immediate object, pleasure, not truth; to romance, by having, for its object, an indefinite instead of a definite pleasure...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should prioritize producing pleasurable (often indefinite) sensations rather than conveying factual truth or didactic instruction. This is an aesthetic criterion that distinguishes poetry from science and from romance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasing the reader is more important than instructing
rubrics_metrics.description: “_ceteris paribus_, he who pleases is of more importance to his fellow-men than he who instructs, since utility is happiness, and pleasure is the end already obtained which instruction is merely the means of obtaining.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should aim primarily to please; didactic aims are secondary. The passage frames aesthetic success in terms of delivering immediate pleasure and happiness to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music (musicality) is essential to poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: “Romance presenting perceptible images with definite, poetry with indefinite sensations, to which end music is an essential, since the comprehension of sweet sound is our most indefinite conception. Music, when combined with a pleasurable idea, is poetry; music, without the idea, is simply music; the idea, without the music, is prose...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The musical qualities of language (sound, rhythm, cadence) are central; poetry requires the union of musicality and idea. Anti-patterns: verse that is merely musical without meaning, or ideas expressed without musical lyricism (prose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making poetry a metaphysical study rather than a passion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Against the subtleties which would make poetry a study—not a passion—it becomes the metaphysician to reason—but the poet to protest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should not be unduly abstruse, metaphysical, or merely intellectualized; prioritize feeling and passion over theoretical subtlety. The author criticizes poets whose work is primarily metaphysical and inaccessible (e.g., extended critique of Coleridge/Wordsworth tendencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination and passion matter more than learning and age
rubrics_metrics.description: “Learning has little to do with the imagination—intellect with the passions—or age with poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarship, erudition, or chronological age are not reliable indicators of poetic genius. Valued qualities are imagination, spontaneity, and passionate feeling rather than mere scholarship or maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy is a central poetic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Delicacy is the poet’s own kingdom—his _El Dorado_.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtle, delicate feeling and expression are prized; poets should cultivate finesse and refinement in tone and sensibility. This supports the broader claim that poetry often deals in nuanced, 'indefinite' sensations rather than coarse didactic statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware over-correctness that kills vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Wordsworth: his increase of judgment made the poetic light fade—'His judgment consequently is too correct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive correctness, over-refinement, or pedantic reasoning can dull poetic vigor. Maintain spontaneity and emotional force; do not let critical correctness supplant imaginative energy.
